lesson.title: Settling In: Meeting Your New Colleagues

concept.explanation_zh: 初次见面时，可以先提一句双方的共同背景，再问一个容易回答的小问题，让对话自然展开。回应对方说的话，比连续抛出问题更像交流。这里的 small talk 指轻松寒暄，并不等于没有意义的谈话。
examples: I think we've exchanged a few emails. It's nice to finally meet you.
How's your week going so far?
I'm still finding my way around. Do you have a favorite lunch spot nearby?
concept.common_mistake_zh: 避免一见面就连续追问薪资、婚姻等私人细节，或把聊天变成面试。询问之前在哪里工作本身并不失礼，关键看关系、语气和时机。先回应一句，再追问一个相关问题：That sounds interesting. How did you get into that?

vocabulary.pronunciation_tip_zh: settle 的重音在第一个音节；第二个音节轻读。in 接着读，不必在两个词之间停顿。
vocabulary.meaning_zh: 逐渐适应新环境，开始感到自在。
vocabulary.explain_in_english: It means to become comfortable in a new place, job, or routine.
vocabulary.usage_note_zh: 搬家、入职、入住新住处时都能用。How are you settling in? 是关心新同事的自然问法。
examples: How are you settling in at the new office?
It took me a couple of weeks to settle in.

vocabulary.pronunciation_tip_zh: ropes 中的 /oʊ/ 是双元音，结尾 /ps/ 要保留；the 在这里通常弱读为 /ðə/。
vocabulary.meaning_zh: 带某人熟悉流程，教某人如何上手。
vocabulary.explain_in_english: It means to teach someone how things work when they are new to a job or activity.
vocabulary.usage_note_zh: 常见于同事之间或非正式培训。someone 可换成 me、you、her 等：Could you show me the ropes?
examples: Maya showed me the ropes during my first week.
I'll show you the ropes before you handle a booking on your own.

vocabulary.term: put a face to the name
vocabulary.pronunciation_tip_zh: face 和 name 都含 /eɪ/；a、to、the 通常弱读，主要信息落在 face 和 name 上。
vocabulary.meaning_zh: 终于把听过或读过的名字与本人对上号。
vocabulary.explain_in_english: It means to meet or see someone after already knowing their name, so you can connect the name with a person.
vocabulary.usage_note_zh: 适合先通过邮件认识、后来首次见面的情况。完全没听过对方名字时不宜这样说。
examples: It's nice to finally put a face to the name after all those emails.
The team photo helped me put a face to the name.

scene.title: Meeting a Colleague You Have Only Emailed
scene.context_zh: 你刚加入一个团队，第一次见到之前通过邮件联系过的同事。将方括号里的姓名和团队名称换成自己的信息；Chris 是示例中的同事。
scene.script_en:
You: Hi, are you Chris? I'm [your name]. We exchanged a few emails about the project last week.
Chris: Oh, hi! It's nice to finally put a face to the name. How are you settling in?
You: Pretty well, thanks. Everyone's been welcoming. I'm still figuring out where everything is, though.
Chris: That takes a little time. Have you found the coffee machine yet?
You: Yes, thankfully! Finding the meeting rooms is another story. I nearly walked into the wrong one this morning.
Chris: I've done that too. The names are confusing. I can show you around after lunch if you're free.
You: That would be great. And could you show me the ropes with the shared calendar? I don't want to book a room that's already taken.
Chris: Of course. It only takes a few minutes. Which team have you joined?
You: The [team name] team. I'll be working on a new project with them.
Chris: Sounds interesting. A few of us are getting lunch downstairs. Would you like to come?
You: I'd love to. Let me grab my bag.
scene.translation_zh:
你：你好，你是 Chris 吗？我是[你的名字]。我们上周通过几封邮件讨论过那个项目。
Chris：哦，你好！终于见到本人了。你适应得怎么样？
你：挺好的，谢谢。大家都很热情。不过，我还在熟悉各个地方的位置。
Chris：这需要一点时间。你找到咖啡机了吗？
你：找到了，幸好！找会议室可就没那么顺利了。今天早上我差点走错。
Chris：我也犯过这个错。那些名字容易弄混。如果你有空，我午饭后可以带你转转。
你：那太好了。另外，你能教我怎么用共享日历吗？我可不想预订已经被占用的会议室。
Chris：当然，只需要几分钟。你加入的是哪个团队？
你：[团队名称]团队。我会和他们一起做一个新项目。
Chris：听起来不错。我们几个人准备去楼下吃午饭。你要一起吗？
你：好啊。等我拿一下包。
scene.practice_tip_zh: 先背自己的台词，再根据同事的回应接话。最后把项目、团队和遇到的小困难换成你的真实情况，脱稿说一遍。

reading.title: The Seat at the End of the Table
reading.text_en:
On my first morning in the new office, I arrived ten minutes early and spent eight of them trying to open the wrong door. By the time someone let me in, my carefully prepared introduction had disappeared from my mind. I managed my name and a smile. That would have to do.

At lunchtime, I took my sandwich to an empty seat at the end of a long table. I was about to put on my headphones when a colleague asked whether the seat beside me was taken. Her name was Nina. We had exchanged emails the week before, but this was our first proper conversation. She asked how I was settling in, and I admitted that the building still felt like a maze.

Instead of offering general advice, Nina drew a tiny map on a paper napkin. She marked the kitchen, the quiet meeting room, and the printer that actually worked. Then she showed me the ropes with the booking system on her phone. None of this took more than five minutes, but it changed the afternoon. I no longer felt that every small question would be an interruption.

I kept the napkin in my notebook. A month later, when another new colleague joined us, I noticed him studying the signs outside the lift. I introduced myself and offered to walk with him. I did not have a brilliant opening line. I simply remembered what it felt like to be new, and how much a little practical kindness could help.
reading.summary_zh: 新同事 Nina 用一张餐巾纸画的小地图和几分钟的实际帮助，让初来乍到的作者安心下来。一个月后，作者将同样的善意传递给另一个新人。

questions.question: Why did Nina's help make such a difference to the writer?
questions.answer: Her specific, practical help made the office easier to navigate and showed the writer that asking small questions was welcome.

questions.question: What did the writer do differently when another new colleague arrived?
questions.answer: The writer took the initiative to introduce themselves and offer help, remembering how it had felt to be new.

editorial_review: Reviewed for teaching accuracy, B2 usefulness, natural dialogue and IPA before first delivery.
